newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Malaysia deepens investment foothold in S.Africa.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia deepens investment foothold in S.Africa.

text.p: Malaysian business strengthened its already impressive investment foothold in South Africa on Wednesday by sealing a multi-billion rand telecommunications deal.

In the biggest direct investment in South Africa yet, Telekom Malaysia Bhd partnered by U.S.-based SBC Communications Inc bought a 30 percent stake in state utility Telkom for $1.261 billion (5.58 billion rand).
The privatisation deal also sets records for the Malaysians.
"Telekom Malaysia is excited about this opportunity in South Africa. It represents Telekom Malaysia's largest overseas investment," said vice-president of corporate strategy Sham Manickan.

Since South Africa's first democratic election in 1994, Malaysians have moved swiftly into the country, becoming its fourth biggest source of foreign revenue behind traditional partners Britain, the United States and Germany.

The Asian state has also brought in the second largest offshore investment since the African National Congress came to power. That deal saw Malaysian state oil company Petronas pay 1.9 billion rand last year for a 30 percent stake in South Africa's Engen Ltd.
Closer trade and diplomatic ties have also been forged between the two nations, culminating this month in President Nelson Mandela's state visit to Malaysia where he secured more lucrative deals.
Businessmen say South Africa's key appeal for Malaysia is its position as a gateway to the rest of Africa.
Announcing the Petronas deal last June, chief executive Dato Hassan Marican said: "We will be using (the Engen acquistion) as a launching pad for us to be involved in the African continent."

Dennis Dykes, chief economist at banking group Nedcor Ltd, endorses that view: "Africa as a whole is the last unexploited region for foreign investment. They want to get a foothold at the right stage before it becomes the vogue."

Initially favouring moves into property developments, Malaysians have also made forays into banking, mining, food and energy industries. Recently they have started pumping funds into emerging black-run businesses.
Malaysia's experience of an empowerment process, similar to South Africa's efforts to redress racial bias, is also seen as a drawcard.
"I think they probably understand South Africa," Dana Becker, head of research at ING Barings, told Reuters.

Some 25 years ago Malaysia adopted an affirmative action programme, including university quotas and preferential share allocations, aimed at giving indigenous Malays a leg-up in a business world dominated by ethnic Chinese.
The two nations also share a common heritage as former British colonies with a multiracial populations. They have Muslim links and English as a business language.
Dykes said the investment drive could also be seen as a "safety net" for a country which, growing at an alarmingly fast rate, might in future find its trade activities curbed.
"It may be part of Malaysia's general diversification drive to put something in Africa which may have good trade access into the European Union and the United States in future decades."
Other major Malaysian investments in South Africa, according to research firm BusinessMap, include:
* Some 435 million rand by the Samrand group, formerly Landmarks Bhd, in mainly property developments and banking;
* Around 300 million by Mycom Bhd in nine investments in industries including granite, food, liquor and hotels, and property;
* Monies from Renong Bhd totalling around 150 million rand for property construction;
* Twenty-four million rand from TA Enterprises Bhd spent on a stockbroking firm and real estate;
* A 190 million investment by Business Focus in a Hilton Hotel in the capital city, Johannesburg; and
* Less than 10 million by the Serting Group in two properties.
-- Johannesburg newsroom 27 11 482 1003
